lessonTitle: Case: SMS codes rerouted to drain German bank accounts (2017)
question: In the 2017 German case, who was best placed to stop the SMS redirection itself?
options: The victims, by installing antivirus on their phones
The mobile operators, by filtering signalling messages at their network edge
The banks, by encrypting their text messages
The newspaper that reported it
explain: SS7 messages travel between operators' core networks; ENISA stresses that subscribers can do very little and that most protection must be done by providers. Phone antivirus cannot see core signalling, and SMS cannot be end-to-end encrypted by the bank. Banks can reduce their reliance on SMS, but only the operator can stop the redirection.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: 5G identity privacy: SUPI, SUCI and ECIES concealment
question: An operator launches 5G but never provisions the home network public key in its USIMs. What does a 5G phone on that network send when asked for its identity?
options: A SUCI using the null-scheme, which contains the MSIN in clear
A SUCI encrypted with a default public key
Nothing: the phone refuses to register
Its 5G-GUTI, which the network can always resolve
explain: TS 33.501 says the phone uses the null-scheme if the home network has not provisioned the public key. The null-scheme returns the input unchanged, so the identity is effectively in clear.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Lawful interception: a built-in wiretap, and the Athens affair
question: In the Athens case, why did Vodafone's operators not see the taps in their tools?
options: The taps were encrypted
The taps were run from a satellite
The rogue software used the switches' interception functions directly, and Vodafone had no interception management system installed to display them
The prime minister's phone was on another network
explain: IEEE Spectrum reports Vodafone had not bought the interception management system, and the rogue code drove the AXE's built-in functions without it, also suppressing the transaction log.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: GNSS: how a receiver finds position and time, and what jamming does
question: A spoofer delays every satellite signal reaching a static timing receiver by the same amount. What does the receiver report?
options: A position far from its real location
No fix at all
A warning that it is being spoofed
The correct position but a wrong time
explain: In the pseudorange equation a common delay is absorbed entirely by the clock term c times b, as the code shows: zero position error, clock off by the delay. A timing-only receiver has no position jump to notice.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
question: Your normalizer computes *Present* using the server clock at index time. A profile indexed on 2025-01-15 with *Sep 2021 to Present* is searched on 2026-10-20. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, Present is stored as a string
Its tenure keeps growing, because tenure is recomputed at query time
The role is double counted
Its tenure is frozen at the index date and is about 21 months short
explain: Index-time resolution freezes Present to 2025-01, so tenure stops growing: Sep 2021 to Jan 2025 is 41 months, while at the query date it is 62. The role also stops counting as current. Store the open end and resolve it against the query's reference date, or re-index regularly.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
question: Which method is **sequential** in the s1 paper's sense?
options: Majority vote over 64 independent samples
Best-of-N with unit tests
Letting the model keep reasoning after it tried to stop, so later tokens build on earlier ones
Running the same prompt on 8 GPUs at once
explain: Sequential means later computation depends on earlier computation, like a longer chain of thought or a revision. The other options are independent attempts (parallel) or just hardware parallelism.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
question: Lookahead search with k = 3 and N = 16 beams is charged how many generations in Snell et al.'s cost protocol?
explain: Lookahead costs N x (k + 1) = 16 x 4 = 64, because each step is also rolled out k steps ahead. That extra cost is one reason it underperformed at equal budget.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Measure it yourself: a test-time scaling harness on GSM8K
question: Why did we estimate each question's difficulty from samples 1 to 32 and measure the methods on samples 33 to 64?
options: Using the same samples would make bins partly sorted by the noise in the very samples being scored, biasing per-bin results
vLLM requires two separate batches of 32
Majority vote cannot use more than 32 samples
Samples 33 to 64 were drawn at a lower temperature
explain: If a question lands in the easiest bin partly because its first samples were lucky, scoring those same samples overstates the bin. Held-out samples give an unbiased read within each bin, as Snell et al.'s cross-validation does for strategy selection.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: In the Titans update, the model sets alpha_t close to 1 at some token. What does that do?
options: Writes this token's value with maximum strength
Clears almost all of the memory before adding the current update
Freezes the memory so this token is ignored
Carries all of the previous surprise into this step
explain: alpha_t multiplies the old memory by (1 - alpha_t). Near 1 that wipes the memory, which is useful at a hard context boundary. Write strength is theta_t; carrying past surprise is eta_t.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
question: A document says "the meeting is in room 4" and later "the meeting moved to room 9", both stored under the same key. Which memory is most likely to answer with a blend of the two?
options: A Mesa layer with no forgetting (gamma = 1)
A delta-rule memory with a unit key and eta = 1
A Mesa layer with a strong forget gate
Titans with alpha near 1 at the second statement
explain: Exact least squares over all past pairs with equal weights finds the average of conflicting values for one key, as the three writes showed: (1, 1.5) for values (2, 1) and (0, 2). The delta rule with eta x |k|^2 = 1 overwrites exactly, a strong forget gate downweights the old fact, and alpha near 1 wipes the old memory before writing.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
question: A colleague proposes a single-magazine design with M = 64 instead of two magazines with M = 32, arguing it uses the same memory and has a lower 1/M. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing, a bigger M always lowers depot traffic
Magazine size must be a power of two smaller than 64
A single magazine can still thrash at its boundary: an alloc-alloc-free-free loop hits the depot on half the calls whatever M is
Two magazines double the number of locks taken per alloc
explain: The 1/M argument only holds when a depot trip leaves you with one full and one empty magazine. With one magazine, a loop straddling the empty/full boundary pays a depot trip every second operation, independent of M.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Three ways to start a hunt: hypothesis, intelligence and data
question: Which hypothesis is ready to hunt?
options: We should look at PowerShell
Our network may contain advanced attackers
Ransomware is a big risk this year
On domain controllers, an account that has never run ntdsutil.exe runs it with the ifm argument; evidence: 30 days of process creation logs with command lines
explain: Only the domain controller hypothesis names a behaviour, a location and the evidence to check, so it can be proved or disproved. The others are topics or worries: useful for the backlog, but not yet hypotheses.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in EDR data II: LSASS, WMI and sensors that go quiet
question: Your silence hunt computes the last event time per device from DeviceProcessEvents over 7 days and flags devices quiet for more than 24 hours. Which compromised machine can it never flag?
options: One whose sensor was disabled 8 days ago and has sent nothing since
One whose last process event was 3 days ago
One whose clock is wrong
One whose sensor stopped 30 hours ago
explain: A device with no events in the window produces no group, so it cannot appear in the output at all. You need to start from the inventory (DeviceInfo or your asset list) and find devices with no matching events: a left anti join. The 30-hour case is exactly what the query does catch.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: From hunt to detection: the FireEye countermeasures
question: The 'Rare process opens LSASS' hunt returns about 41 matches a week, almost all explainable, and the SOC's budget for one rule is 5 a week. What should it become?
options: A supplemental, scheduled hunt that a person reviews weekly while it is tuned, with known-benign programs recorded
A blocking rule that kills any process opening LSASS
Nothing; delete it because it found no intrusion
A production alert, because credential theft is severe
explain: At 41 a week it would swamp the queue and teach analysts to ignore it, but it still covers an important technique. FireEye's 'supplemental' state is exactly this: needs environment-specific tuning, used in hunting workflows. Tune with known-benign entries until volume and precision justify promotion. Blocking all LSASS access would break security and backup agents.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The intelligence cycle and intelligence requirements
question: Two weeks after a briefing, the CISO says it was 'interesting' but nobody changed anything. In the cycle, which step most clearly failed or was skipped?
options: Collection
Planning and direction
Processing and exploitation
Encryption of the report
explain: A product that changes no decision usually answered a question nobody needed answered: the requirement was never agreed in planning and direction. Feedback (step 5) is how you discover this, but the fix is upstream: agree the PIR and the decision it serves before collecting.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners
question: A phishing email came from a real supplier's mailbox that attackers had taken over. In the Diamond Model, what is that mailbox?
options: Type 1 infrastructure, owned by the adversary
Type 2 infrastructure, controlled by an unwitting intermediary, and also a victim asset in an earlier event
The adversary feature
A capability
explain: The paper's Type 2 infrastructure includes compromised email accounts controlled by witting or unwitting intermediaries, and notes that a victim asset in one event can be leveraged as infrastructure in later events. Treating the supplier as the adversary would be a classic mistake.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Analytic tradecraft: bias and competing hypotheses
question: In an ACH matrix, an item of evidence is consistent with all four hypotheses. What does Heuer say about it?
options: It is the strongest evidence because everything agrees with it
It has no diagnostic value for choosing between them and can be set aside in step 4
It proves all four hypotheses
It should be counted twice
explain: Diagnosticity is about telling hypotheses apart. Heuer's example is a high temperature: useful to know the patient is ill, useless to decide which illness. Evidence consistent with every hypothesis does not move their relative likelihood.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: What a threat model is: four questions before the code
question: Which statement best describes a vulnerability, in the 1999 Microsoft definitions?
options: An action an intruder takes against the system
Any potential occurrence that could harm the system
A characteristic that makes it possible for a threat to occur
The person or group that attacks the system
explain: A threat is the potential harm, an attack is the action, and a vulnerability is the weakness that lets the threat happen. The attacker themselves is usually called a threat agent or threat actor.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE per element: from a diagram to a threat list
question: A new feature adds one external partner API and one data flow to it. How many new STRIDE-per-element prompts appear?
explain: An external entity gets S and R (2) and a data flow gets T, I and D (3), so 5 new prompts.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles II: least privilege, two keys and shared parts
question: A nightly backup job runs as a domain administrator (full control of every Windows machine in the company) because "it needs to read everything". The backup software has a remote code execution bug. Which principle would have limited the damage most?
options: Open design
Psychological acceptability
Economy of mechanism
Least privilege: a read-only backup account cannot create users or change systems
explain: The job needs to read files, not administer the domain. With least privilege, the bug gives the attacker read access to backed-up data, which is bad, rather than control of every machine. (Keep that data narrow too: a backup that includes the domain's password database is nearly as bad as admin.)

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: A full threat model of a small web app
question: Which pair of threats did BOTH the attack tree and the ranked STRIDE threat list flag as the cheapest or most urgent?
options: T5 and T7
T4 and T6
T8 and T9
T1 (password replay) and T2 (IDOR)
explain: The attack tree's cheapest branches were password replay (200) and the URL trick (500); the ratings of the STRIDE threat list put both at High. Agreement between two techniques raises confidence that the obvious threats are covered.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
question: DRAM holds a job's hot pages and CXL is full of warm pages touched every few seconds. Another 50 GB of pages are touched about once per hour. Where should those 50 GB go?
options: SSD swap (with zswap in front): one major fault per page per hour is negligible
Move warm CXL pages to SSD swap so the hourly pages fit on CXL
DRAM, by demoting some hot pages to CXL
Nowhere: tiering cannot help this job
explain: Cost is access rate times miss cost. An hourly page pays one 10 to 40 us fault per hour, which is nothing; a warm page on swap would fault every few seconds. The coldest pages belong in the lowest tier.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
question: What does zero-shot forecasting with Chronos mean?
options: Forecasting with zero horizon
Forecasting a series the model was not trained on, without fitting to it
Training on zero-valued series only
Using no seasonal component
explain: Chronos is pretrained on a large corpus. Zero-shot means applying it directly to a new series with no training on that dataset. The Chronos paper reports comparable and occasionally better accuracy than models trained on those datasets.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Resumption and 0-RTT: faster, and replayable
question: Which statement about TLS 1.3 resumption is correct?
options: Resumption always skips the key exchange, so it never has forward secrecy
With the psk_dhe_ke mode, a resumed connection still performs a fresh (EC)DHE exchange, so its main traffic keeps forward secrecy; only 0-RTT data lacks it
0-RTT data is protected against replay by the Finished message
Tickets contain the server's certificate private key
explain: psk_dhe_ke mixes a new (EC)DHE secret into the Handshake Secret, so later keys do not depend only on the ticket. Early data comes before that exchange and so depends on the PSK alone.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Chains and roots: how a browser validates a certificate
question: Why do CAs issue leaf certificates from intermediates instead of directly from the root?
options: So the root key can stay offline, and a compromised or retired intermediate can be replaced without changing trust stores on every device
Roots cannot sign leaf certificates
Intermediates are faster to verify
Because browsers ignore root signatures
explain: Roots are expensive to replace: they live in operating systems and devices that update slowly. Keeping them offline and delegating day-to-day issuance to intermediates limits the blast radius of a compromise.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate Transparency: logging every certificate
question: What does an SCT actually prove at the moment the browser sees it?
options: That the certificate is already in the Merkle tree
That the domain owner approved the certificate
That the certificate is not revoked
That a log signed a promise to include the certificate within its maximum merge delay; auditing later checks the promise was kept
explain: An SCT is a timestamped promise. Inclusion is checked afterwards by auditors through Merkle proofs; a log that breaks its promises is distrusted.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Heartbleed: trusting a length field in OpenSSL
question: After patching OpenSSL, why did operators also have to replace their certificates' private keys?
options: The patch changed the key format
Certificates expired at the same time
The private key may already have leaked through heartbeat responses, and patching does not un-leak it; a new key (and revoking the old certificate) was the only safe assumption
Browsers required new keys for TLS 1.2
explain: Exploitation left no trace in normal logs, so operators could not prove their key had not been read. Rekeying, not just reissuing, was required.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
question: Why is BLOCK_SIZE declared as tl.constexpr instead of a normal int argument?
options: Because tl.arange needs a compile-time shape, so the value is baked into the compiled kernel
Because Python ints cannot be passed to GPU kernels
Because constexpr arguments are stored in shared memory
Because it makes the value changeable while the kernel runs
explain: Block shapes must be known when the kernel is compiled. Triton includes constexpr values in the kernel's specialization key (the values its cache of compiled kernels is looked up by), so each distinct BLOCK_SIZE gets its own compiled binary. Ordinary ints like n_elements are passed at run time.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
question: Why does a unified model beat an LLM that calls a separate image generator through a text prompt, for a request like "make the dog in the previous picture wear a hat"?
options: The unified model has more parameters in total
Diffusion models cannot generate dogs
The generator only sees the prompt string, not the earlier image, while a unified model attends to the earlier image tokens directly
Tool calls are not allowed during generation
explain: The bottleneck is information, not size. In a pipeline the generator conditions only on what fits in the prompt. In a unified model the earlier image is part of the same context, so the new image can attend to it.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
question: A team needs one model that reads screenshots with small text and also generates images that must preserve fine detail, and can afford extra architecture. Which combination best fits the evidence in this course?
options: One shared VQ tokenizer with a causal mask, for simplicity
Discrete tokens at f = 32 to save context
A separate semantic encoder for understanding plus continuous latents with a diffusion or flow loss for generation
Text-only LLM with an external OCR tool and no image generation
explain: Chameleon's paper flags OCR as a weakness of discrete tokens, Janus shows a dedicated understanding encoder lifts MMBench from 35.0 to 69.4, and Transfusion shows continuous latents beat discrete tokens on generation at equal compute. BAGEL combines these choices.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
question: A unikernel's guest boot takes 0.3 ms and total VM start takes 40 ms on standard QEMU. What will most reduce cold-start latency?
options: Removing more micro-libraries from the image
Using a faster memory allocator
Moving from KVM to emulation mode
Switching to a lightweight VMM such as Firecracker or Solo5
explain: The guest is under 1% of the 40 ms. Unikraft's measurements put total boot at about 3 ms on Firecracker and Solo5 versus about 40 ms on QEMU, so the VMM choice is the lever.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Hands-on: build, boot and measure a unikernel
question: Your Mirage unikernel crashes inside its HTTP handler and you want a debugger and a profiler. Which target do you build?
options: hvt, because only the VM build has the real network stack
unix (or macosx), because the same code then runs as an ordinary process
virtio, because it has the most devices
None: unikernels cannot be debugged
explain: Mirage builds the same application against different device implementations. The Unix target produces a normal executable, so ordinary debuggers and profilers work; you switch to hvt for deployment.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
question: hnswlib prefetches `vector_of(data[j + 1])`. For a 768-d fp32 vector, what does that one instruction bring toward the cache?
options: All 3,212 bytes of the next neighbor's block
One 64-byte cache line at the start of the next neighbor's vector
The whole neighbor list of the next neighbor
Nothing on ARM builds without SSE, and everything on x86
explain: A prefetch hint covers the cache line containing the address. Here that is the first line of the vector. The remaining lines rely on the hardware stream prefetcher once the distance loop starts reading.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Quickstart, end to end: data, reward, launch, logs and export
question: A new GSM8K-style run shows critic/score/mean at exactly 0 from step 1 while response_length looks normal. Which two things should you check first?
options: The learning rate and the KL coefficient
Whether data_source routes to the scorer you meant, and whether responses contain the answer in the form that scorer extracts
The number of GPUs and the rollout tensor-parallel size
Whether the checkpoint directory exists
explain: A score of exactly 0 before any learning means the scorer never matched. Either data_source sent rows to a different scorer (say GSM8K's strict '#### number' rule for data that answers in LaTeX boxes), or the prompt never asks for the format the scorer extracts. Optimizer settings cannot make step 1 zero.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and tuning verl in practice
question: A colocated run trains fine but crashes with out-of-memory right when the first rollout starts after an update. Which setting is the most likely culprit?
options: rollout.gpu_memory_utilization is set too high for GPUs that also hold training state
data.train_batch_size is not divisible by the number of GPUs
algorithm.adv_estimator is set to grpo
trainer.balance_batch is enabled
explain: At the transition the rollout reclaims its weight and KV cache memory on GPUs where the training engine may still hold parameters or optimizer state. For vLLM, gpu_memory_utilization is a fraction of total memory, so a value that ignores the colocated trainer overcommits. Lowering it or enabling offload addresses the transition.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
question: A team doubles the frame rate from 1 fps to 2 fps and also switches from 196 to 49 tokens per frame. What happens to the total token count for the same video?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
It drops to a quarter
explain: Total = frames x tokens per frame. Frames go up 2x, tokens per frame go down 4x (196 to 49), so the total is 2/4 = 0.5 of the original. More temporal detail can be bought with less spatial detail.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
question: MovieChat's short-term memory holds 18 frames of 32 tokens and consolidates to 2 frames. How many visual tokens does each consolidation add to long-term memory?
explain: 2 frames x 32 tokens = 64 tokens. The 18 x 32 = 576 tokens in the buffer shrink 9x, and long-term memory is capped at 256 frames, 8,192 tokens.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Latent actions: a controller learned from unlabelled video
question: Which part of the latent action model is still used when a person plays Genie?
options: The encoder, to infer actions from the player's screen
The decoder, to render each frame
Only the VQ codebook, indexed by the integer the player chooses
Nothing; the dynamics model takes raw keyboard codes
explain: Apart from the VQ codebook, the entire LAM is discarded at inference. The player's integer in [0, 8) selects a code vector, whose embedding conditions the dynamics model.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: VT-x and AMD-V: VM entries, VM exits and the control structure
question: Which VMCS area does the CPU load from on every VM exit, so that the hypervisor regains control in a known state?
options: Guest-state area
Host-state area
VM-exit information fields
VM-entry control fields
explain: Per the SDM, processor state is loaded from the host-state area on VM exits. The guest-state area is where the guest's registers are saved; the exit information fields only describe why the exit happened.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Device emulation: the attack surface the guest controls
question: A guest-reachable QEMU device crashes on an assert, but only when the guest kernel sends a malformed command. According to QEMU's policy, how is it classified, and why might a cloud provider still care?
options: A security bug in all cases
Not a bug, because asserts are intended
A security bug only under TCG

A hardening bug, since guest root causes a self-inflicted denial of service; a provider still cares because a crash may hide a memory bug, and it should check that only the tenant's own VM is affected
explain: QEMU treats guest-root-only aborts as self-inflicted DoS. That is fair when the only victim is the guest's own VM. Providers still fix them: the crash path may also reach memory corruption, and shared host resources must stay unaffected.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: the 2025 ESXi escape chain, VMSA-2025-0004
question: In the double-fetch toy, which change fixes the bug?
options: Reading the length from shared memory once into host memory, then checking and using that copy
Checking the length twice
Adding a sleep between the reads
Making BUF_LEN larger
explain: The guest can change shared memory at any time. Only a private copy is stable between check and use. Checking twice still leaves a window; a sleep widens it; a bigger buffer just moves the limit.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Attestation: proving what is running before you send it secrets
question: A verifier checks the report's signature chain and the MEASUREMENT, but never looks at REPORT_DATA. What can a malicious host do?
options: Nothing; the signature covers everything
Change the measurement without breaking the signature
Replay a genuine report from an earlier boot of the right image to a fake VM, and receive the secret
Disable SMT
explain: REPORT_DATA binds the report to this request and to the key the secret will be sealed to. Without that check, any old valid report proves nothing about the VM asking now.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
question: Why does DeiT resize position embeddings with bicubic rather than bilinear interpolation?
options: Bicubic is faster on GPUs
Bilinear interpolation shrinks the vectors' norm, and short embeddings hurt the pretrained network
Bilinear cannot resize a 14x14 grid to 24x24 because 24 is not a multiple of 14
Bicubic interpolates the CLS embedding too, which bilinear cannot
explain: DeiT's stated reason is the norm: averaging neighbors shortens vectors, and those low-norm embeddings are out of distribution for the pretrained blocks. Both methods handle any target size, and the CLS embedding is not interpolated at all; it is kept as is.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Binning: one 7-DoF action becomes seven tokens
question: A dimension has bounds [-0.05, 0.05] m and 256 uniform bins. For an action inside the bounds, what is the largest possible decoding error?
options: 0.39 mm, one full bin
0.195 mm, half a bin
0.05 m, half the range
Zero, because the token stores the exact value
explain: The bin width is 0.1 m / 256 = 0.39 mm. Decoding returns the bin center, so the worst case is a value at a bin edge: half a bin, 0.195 mm.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
question: A Diffusion Policy user raises the execution horizon from 8 to 64 steps on a task where objects get bumped. Success drops. Why?
options: Longer chunks are less smooth
The diffusion model cannot predict more than 16 steps
Longer execution horizons increase the number of denoising steps per action
The robot executes many actions without looking, so it reacts slowly when the scene changes
explain: Executing more steps open-loop improves consistency but delays the next observation. Diffusion Policy's ablation found too long a horizon hurts because of slow reaction time, with 8 steps best for most tasks.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: VQGAN: perceptual and adversarial losses for 256-token images
question: Why did the VQGAN paper target 256 tokens per image rather than, say, 1024?
options: The codebook had only 256 entries
256 was the longest sequence they could feasibly train a 307M GPT-2 medium on with a 12 GB GPU
The perceptual loss only works on 16 x 16 grids
Longer sequences always give worse reconstructions
explain: The paper states 16 x 16 was the maximum feasible length for GPT-2 medium on a 12 GB GPU. The perceptual and adversarial losses were what made reconstructions at that strong compression good enough.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
question: Your reference backend declares `_cudagraph_support = AttentionCGSupport.NEVER` and you start it with the default `-O2`. What happens?
options: Startup fails, because FULL_AND_PIECEWISE needs at least UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE
vLLM captures full graphs anyway and replays them with stale Python lists
vLLM silently picks FLASH_ATTN instead
vLLM logs a warning and falls back to PIECEWISE graphs, so attention runs eagerly while the other pieces still replay as graphs
explain: The default mode only asks for full graphs on decode batches, and the resolver downgrades that to PIECEWISE when support is NEVER and attention is a splitting op. Only modes that ask for full graphs on mixed batches raise an error with NEVER. Selection never swaps a backend you named.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend
question: Which layout puts every KV head of one token next to each other inside a block?
options: LBHNC
LBNHC
LHBNC
BHLNC
explain: In LBNHC the order inside a block is N, then H, then C, so for a fixed token all heads are adjacent. LBHNC and BHLNC keep each head's tokens together instead, and LHBNC moves heads outside the block.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Training the bridge: LLaVA's two stages and Flamingo's cross-attention
question: Flamingo initializes each gate scalar alpha to 0. What does that buy at the start of training?
options: The visual features are ignored forever unless alpha is reset
It forces the Perceiver Resampler to output 64 tokens
The new blocks contribute nothing, so the model initially behaves exactly like the pretrained language model, which stabilizes training
It makes cross-attention cheaper to compute
explain: $\tanh(0) = 0$, so the added block's output is multiplied by zero and the residual stream is untouched. Alpha is learnable, so the model gradually opens the gate as it learns to use the image; the paper reports this improves stability and final performance.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Why a lock-free CAS loop can starve one thread
question: In the simulation, a CAS-loop increment at 16 threads averaged 3.83 attempts and the worst observed was 51. What can you conclude about its worst case?
options: It is at most 51 attempts
It is about 4 attempts on average, so it is wait-free in practice
No finite bound exists: some schedule makes a thread retry forever
It is bounded by 16 attempts, one per competing thread
explain: The simulation only samples schedules. The adversarial timeline shows a schedule where B fails every time, so the operation is lock-free but not wait-free. Observed maxima are a property of the sample, not of the algorithm.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
question: With MAX_PATIENCE = 10, at most how many times does wfqueue's `enqueue` call `enq_fast` before switching to the slow path?
options: Unbounded
explain: The loop calls enq_fast first and only then tests and decrements p. Calls 1 to 10 fail with p at 10 down to 1, each passing the test; call 11 fails with p at 0, the test fails and p drops to -1. So 11 fast attempts, then enq_slow.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
question: What ACC does a forecast that always predicts climatology get?
options: 1, because climatology is unbiased
0.6, the usefulness threshold
0, because its anomalies are all zero
It depends on the RMSE
explain: ACC correlates anomalies from climatology. A climatology forecast has zero anomaly everywhere, so it carries no pattern information and scores 0 by definition (WeatherBench 2 states this).

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: The intercepting proxy: Burp Suite and ZAP as a workflow
question: Why must Burp's CA certificate be trusted by the browser for HTTPS testing?
options: It speeds up the TLS handshake
It lets Burp decrypt traffic recorded earlier
Burp presents its own certificate for each site, and the browser would otherwise reject it as an impersonation
Servers require it before they accept proxied requests
explain: Interception means two TLS connections. The browser's side ends at Burp, which signs a certificate for each host with its own CA. Without that CA in the trust store, the browser correctly warns that something is impersonating the site.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
question: Two failed logins return the same message and status, but the response for an existing account takes 120 ms and for an unknown one 3 ms. What does this show?
options: Nothing, since the messages match
The server is overloaded
Timing reveals which accounts exist, probably because the slow password hash runs only for known users
The account is locked
explain: A consistent timing gap is an enumeration channel. The usual cause is that only known users go through the slow password hash; the fix is to do equivalent work for unknown users, as login_fixed does.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Blind SSRF, out-of-band checks and server-side browsers
question: A link-preview feature validates that submitted URLs resolve to public addresses, then renders them in headless Chrome. Why is that validation insufficient?
options: Headless Chrome ignores the URL
Public addresses cannot host web pages
The browser follows redirects and loads subresources and scripts, so later requests can reach internal addresses the check never saw
DNS cannot be checked from servers
explain: The check covers only the first request. A real browser makes many more, chosen by the page. Only a control on every outbound connection, such as an egress proxy or network isolation, covers them all.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
question: Which step-to-reproduce line is best?
options: Change the id to someone else's and you will see their data
Run my script against all ids from 1 to 100000
As account B (created with my alias), send GET /api/orders/1044, an order created by my account A; response 200 contains A's address
See attached screenshot
explain: It names the identity, the exact request, the object's owner (also you) and the observable result. Changing to 'someone else's' id touches other users, a script over all ids is mass access, and a bare screenshot gives the triager nothing to repeat.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through
question: A page on evil.example contains `` and runs `fetch("https://bank.example/balance")`. With no CORS headers from bank.example, what happens?
options: Both are blocked; nothing is sent to bank.example
The image is blocked but the fetch succeeds
Both succeed, because GET requests are always readable
The image displays; the fetch request is sent but the script cannot read the balance
explain: Embedding an image is allowed cross-origin, so the logo shows. The fetch is sent too (SOP does not stop sending), but without an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header naming evil.example the browser withholds the response body from the script.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS with credentials, and the misconfigurations that leak data
question: A browser makes a cross-origin `fetch` with `credentials: "include"`. The response has `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What happens?
options: The browser blocks the script from reading the response
The script reads the response, since * allows everyone
The browser retries without cookies
The server is forced to resend with the exact origin
explain: With credentials, the wildcard is not acceptable: the server must name the exact origin. The browser sees * and withholds the response, reporting a CORS error in the console. This rule exists to stop accidental exposure of personal data to every site.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: postMessage: talking across origins on purpose, and safely
question: Why is `popup.postMessage(secret, "*")` risky even though you opened the popup yourself?
options: The popup may have been navigated to another origin, and * delivers the message to whatever origin it now has
Because * encrypts the message with a weak key
It is not risky if the popup was opened by your own code
Because * sends the message to every open tab
explain: MDN warns that a malicious site can change a window's location without your knowledge. With a specific targetOrigin, the browser drops the message if the window is no longer on that origin; with * it delivers the secret to whoever is there now.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The map: which bug class gets around which rule
question: A forum lets users post images. An attacker posts an image URL that points at `https://bank.example/transfer?to=attacker&amount=500`. The bank changes money on a GET. Which rule would have stopped the browser from attaching the user's bank cookie?
options: Same-origin policy
HSTS
SameSite=Lax or Strict on the bank's session cookie
Subresource Integrity
explain: The image request is cross-origin embedding, which SOP allows, and here it triggers a state change on the server. Under Lax or Strict the cookie is not sent on a cross-site image request, so the bank sees an anonymous request. The deeper bug is changing state on GET, which the CSRF material covers.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
question: A folder's DACL is: (1) Allow Users: Read, (2) Deny Interns: Read. Intern Sam is in both Users and Interns and asks to read. What happens?
options: Denied, because deny always wins regardless of order
Denied implicitly, because two ACEs conflict
Granted, because ACE 1 grants every requested right and the walk stops before the deny
Granted only if Sam is an administrator
explain: The access check stops as soon as all requested rights are granted. ACE 1 grants read, so the deny is never reached. This is why the canonical order puts explicit denies first.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: LSASS: why attackers dump its memory, and how Windows protects it
question: An attacker has a standard (non-admin) user's shell on a laptop. Can they read LSASS memory to steal hashes?
options: Yes, any process can read any other process
Yes, because LSASS runs at low integrity
Not directly: reading LSASS memory requires administrator or SYSTEM, so they first need to escalate
Only if the user is in Remote Desktop Users
explain: ATT&CK notes LSASS credential material is harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM. That is why privilege escalation usually comes before credential dumping.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Event IDs that tell an intrusion story: 4688, 4720, 7045, 1102
question: Which pair of events, close together, most strongly suggests a backdoor administrator account was created?
options: 4720 then 4732 (added to Administrators)
explain: 4720 is account creation and 4732 is a member added to a security-enabled local group. Together they describe a new account being made a local admin.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Patch Tuesday and PrintNightmare: closing holes on a schedule
question: MS17-010 shipped on 14 March 2017; WannaCry hit on 12 May. What does that gap teach?
options: Microsoft was too slow to patch
Patches cause outbreaks
The window that matters is between a fix's release and its installation; organisations that patched within weeks were not hit by this route
Cumulative updates skip older fixes
explain: The fix existed 59 days before WannaCry. The machines that fell were the ones that had not installed it, which is why patch speed is a core security metric.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA2: from passphrase to PMK to the 4-way handshake
question: Why does the client's message 2 carry a MIC?
options: To prove to the AP that the client knows the PMK, using the KCK derived from it
To carry the GTK
To reset the replay counter
To encrypt the SNonce
explain: Only someone who knows the PMK can derive the right KCK and compute a MIC the AP will accept. That is the client's half of mutual authentication; message 3's MIC is the AP's half.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: KRACK and FragAttacks: when the standard itself is wrong
question: After KRACK was announced, a home user changed their Wi-Fi password but did not update their phone. Are they protected?
options: No: KRACK never needed the password; the unpatched phone still reinstalls keys and reuses nonces
Yes, if the new password is long
Only if they also hid the SSID
Yes, the attacker now lacks the password
explain: The attack manipulates when an already-negotiated key gets installed. The password is irrelevant, as the KRACK FAQ says. Only patching the client's handshake logic fixes it.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: iOS: code signing, sandbox, Secure Enclave and BlastDoor
question: An attacker gains code execution inside the iOS kernel. According to Apple's design, what should still be protected?
options: Only App Store apps
Only files in the Documents folder
Nothing; the kernel controls everything
Keys held by the Secure Enclave, which is isolated from the application processor and designed for this case
explain: Apple's guide states the Secure Enclave is designed to keep sensitive data secure even when the Application Processor kernel is compromised. The attacker may use the device, but cannot extract keys that never leave the enclave.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
question: A tester installs a proxy's CA certificate in the phone's user certificate store, then sees an Android app's HTTPS traffic in clear. The app targets API 34 and has no network security config. What does that indicate?
options: The app's own code overrides validation (for example a trust-all trust manager or custom TLS stack), because the default config for API 28+ trusts only system CAs
The proxy broke TLS 1.3
The phone is rooted
Normal behaviour for all apps
explain: Apps targeting Android 7.0 (API 24) or later do not trust user-added CAs by default, and for API 28+ the default base-config also forbids cleartext. If a user CA is accepted, something in the app changed the default.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Lockdown Mode, stalkerware and tracker abuse
question: A person finds an unknown AirTag in their bag and turns off Bluetooth on their iPhone. Does that stop the AirTag's owner from seeing where it is?
options: No: other phones nearby still relay its location; Apple's guidance is to disable the tracker itself, with personal safety in mind
Yes, if Location Services is also off
Only on Android
Yes, AirTags need the victim's Bluetooth
explain: Apple's support page says turning off Bluetooth or Location Services does not prevent the owner from seeing the location. The tracker must be disabled following the onscreen instructions, considering the safety implications.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
question: A task keeps waking a partner task, which wakes it back, forever. Without a cap, what goes wrong with the LIFO slot?
options: Nothing, both tasks get CPU time
The two tasks could take turns in the LIFO slot and starve everything in the local queue; Tokio disables the slot after 3 uses in a row
The tasks are stolen by other workers
The global queue overflows
explain: The LIFO slot always runs before the local queue. Two tasks ping-ponging through it would monopolize the worker, so Tokio disables it after 3 consecutive uses until a task from elsewhere runs.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data
question: Your WSD run uses a 2% linear cooldown, and the final model is noticeably worse than a cosine baseline of the same length. What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise the peak LR so the stable stage makes more progress
Skip the cooldown and use the last stable checkpoint
Switch the cooldown to an LR increase
Lengthen the cooldown to roughly 10 to 20% of training, or at least enough absolute steps
explain: A very short cooldown leaves the hill component frozen in place (MiniCPM: 2.5% falls short, 10% enough; Hägele: gains plateau near 20%). A higher peak LR would only raise the hill further.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Other ways to drop the end date: averaging, schedule-free, theory
question: A teammate switches to Schedule-Free AdamW, keeps the LR and weight decay tuned for cosine AdamW, and evaluates the parameters stored in the model during training. Which two problems should you point out?
options: None: Schedule-Free needs no tuning and the stored parameters are the average
Schedule-Free needs a cosine schedule on top, and it doubles memory
It cannot use warmup, and checkpoints must be saved in train mode
The LR and weight decay need a new sweep, and without optimizer.eval() the model holds y, the gradient point, rather than the average x
explain: The authors report the best LR and weight decay differ from scheduled runs, and their code stores y in the parameter buffer during training; optimizer.eval() swaps in x for evaluation and checkpointing. Warmup is still used, and memory matches AdamW.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
question: An engineer benchmarks MSG_ZEROCOPY between two processes on one machine over 127.0.0.1 and sees no gain. Most likely reason?
options: MSG_ZEROCOPY only works for UDP
The SO_ZEROCOPY option resets on loopback
Packets looped to a local socket always incur a deferred copy
Loopback has no error queue
explain: The kernel converts zero-copy packets to private copies on paths that loop back to local sockets, to bound how long pages stay pinned. The docs warn that such a test will not show any improvement; benchmark between two hosts.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
question: A team measured p_cf with a zero-shot prompt, then switched to an 8-shot prompt with more technology examples and kept the old p_cf. What is the bug?
options: None; p_cf depends only on the model weights
p_cf should have been measured on the test set
Calibration only applies to zero-shot prompts
The bias is contextual: new examples change majority and recency bias, so p_cf must be re-measured with the new prompt
explain: Zhao et al. stress that the error is contextual: a different choice, order, or format of examples changes the content-free prediction. Adding technology examples would likely push the model further toward technology, which the stale p_cf does not account for.
